snippet.description:
You can now interact with OpenAI directly through Azure AI Studio. Learn more about Microsoft Azure AI Studio here: https://aka.ms/AdrianAI

In this video I’m going to cover Azure AI Studio, which will be useful if you’re looking to build something a bit more complex as either a beginner or professional developer at a company.

There will be 5 parts to this video:

1. What is Azure AI Studio
2. Create a model on top of Azure OpenAI
3. Import Data to a Model
4. Configure and Deploy Model
5. API use of the model for a Project

I’d also like to thank Microsoft for sponsoring this video, a lot of what we do today will be built on top of the Microsoft Azure service, so if you want to learn more, I’ll add links in the description to the project.

Azure AI Studio is the combination of tools such as Azure OpenAI, Machine Learning and other AI services like speech, vision, etc in a central place. With it:

- I am able to deploy AI models for deploying and testing AI models on top of the Azure OpenAI service.
- I can add custom data sources to help prompting, such as a database, file or document, or even web address.
- I can define prompts to work almost like a flow chart, this prompt flow lets you create more customization for the models and how they function
- I can integrated content safety filters to help mitigate problems or harm depending on the type of solution you’re building
- I can combine multiple AI capabilities to produce a much more advanced generative AI solution.

snippet.title: Most people get these 3 AI terms wrong
snippet.description:
#AI hallucination is the flip side of creativity. That's the first of three terms most people misunderstand.

Term 1: Hallucination. The same mechanism that produces wrong answers is what generates creative writing, ideas, and novel connections. The real question is whether your task needs creativity or accuracy. Turning off web search in #ChatGPT or Claude gives you more creativity. Turning it on gives you more accuracy.

Term 2: Context window. Think of it as a fixed-size whiteboard. Once it's full, the AI drops older information to fit new input. If your AI starts giving weird answers mid-conversation, just start a new chat.

Term 3: Tokens. This is why free plans have usage limits. AI breaks your words into chunks called tokens, and every chunk costs usage. Better prompts mean fewer tokens, so you get more out of your plan before hitting the cap.

snippet.title: Stop perfecting your prompt. Do this instead
snippet.description:
3 (more) common #AI terms most people don’t know:

Term 1: Grounding.
Without it, AI answers from memory, which may or may not be correct. Hand it the actual document and say "answer from this," and now the response is grounded in something real. Whenever accuracy matters, give the AI something to reference.

Term 2: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation).
Without RAG, the AI writes from memory. With RAG, it goes to the library first, pulls the relevant sources, then generates its answer. The rule of thumb: if an AI tool cites its sources, it most likely uses #RAG. If it doesn't, it's guessing.

Term 3: Context engineering.
Prompt engineering focuses on writing a good prompt (task, context, tone). Context engineering focuses on assembling everything the AI needs: background, examples, constraints. Spend your time on the context, not the wording.
